claims.text: A high-entropy alloy is currently used as the intermediate layer in plasma-facing reactor components.
Adding copper during processing will form uniformly dispersed nanoscale copper-rich precipitates in the high-entropy alloy.
The intended operating-temperature range is approximately 400–600°C.
The alloy will experience cyclic thermal loading and mechanical stresses typical of plasma-facing environments.
Well-dispersed nanoscale copper-rich precipitates will provide enhanced heat-conduction pathways.
Well-dispersed nanoscale copper-rich precipitates will stabilize grain boundaries.
Copper-rich precipitates will enhance thermal transport by providing additional conduction paths across the microstructure.
The small size of the precipitates will prevent their coarsening under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading.
The small precipitate size will prevent embrittlement and preserve structural integrity.
The copper-modified alloy will have a higher heat-transfer coefficient than the unmodified alloy.
The copper-modified alloy will maintain or closely match the mechanical strength of the unmodified alloy.
The copper-modified alloy will maintain or closely match the microstructural robustness of the unmodified alloy.
The proposed effect will hold during thermal and mechanical cycling at 400–600°C under loading typical of intermediate reactor components.
Extreme thermal cycling or long-term radiation damage may destabilize the precipitates and alter the proposed mechanism.
The long-term stability of the nanoscale precipitates under extended radiation exposure and extreme mechanical cycling is uncertain.
